Chapter 9: Integrating New Behaviors into Organizational Culture
Think about this—personal change is powerful on its own, but it becomes even more impactful when it starts to shape the culture of an entire team or organization. When leaders show humility, stay open-minded, and really commit to growing, they set a tone that everyone can feel. Suddenly, continuous improvement isn’t just a buzzword—it’s how things are done.
You’ve probably heard the phrase, “culture is the way we do things around here.” It’s true. Culture gets built from all those little moments—tiny actions, daily conversations, and small choices that add up over time. When leaders make a habit of giving credit, asking for feedback, or even admitting their own mistakes, they’re sending a clear message about what really matters.
So, how can you weave new behaviors into the fabric of your organization?
Here are a few simple but powerful ideas:
First, try publicly recognizing and rewarding the kinds of behaviors you want to see more of. It could be as easy as a shoutout in a meeting, or a quick note of appreciation.
Next, build in chances for feedback and learning—formally, through workshops or training, but also informally, like quick check-ins or open conversations.
Encourage people to talk openly about challenges and setbacks, instead of hiding them. That’s how real learning happens.
And don’t forget to add growth-oriented habits into your routines—maybe you start each team meeting by inviting everyone’s input, or you make space for team debriefs where people can share what they’ve learned.
Imagine a leader who kicks off every meeting by asking for ideas from the whole team, or maybe shares a lesson they picked up from a recent mistake. Little things like this, done over and over, become part of your group’s identity. They start to shape how people connect and tackle problems together.
But here’s something to watch out for—sometimes there are bigger, systemic barriers that can get in the way of change. Maybe it’s outdated policies, or performance metrics that just don’t align with your new direction. Addressing these roadblocks might mean tweaking processes, updating policies, or offering extra training and resources to support everyone as they try new ways of working.
The impact of personal change can ripple out in ways you might not expect. As more people adopt new habits, the whole organization becomes more collaborative, more innovative, and better equipped to handle whatever comes next. Before you know it, your workplace isn’t just somewhere people clock in—it’s a real community, focused on learning and growth.
